headline: Government Defends Economic Record as Forecasts Weaken and Surplus Pushed Back
summary: Parliament was dominated by a tense economic debate following the release of the Half-Year Economic and Fiscal Update, which revealed slower growth and a delayed return to surplus. The Government defended its management, citing underlying positive signs, while the Opposition attacked what it called broken promises on the economy and cost of living. The day also saw the final passage of a controversial electoral law and the introduction of major legislation to replace the Resource Management Act.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Faces Scrutiny Over Weaker Economic Forecasts in Half-Year Update
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The government's latest economic report card forecasts slower growth and a later return to surplus, affecting household finances and the funding of public services.
topicSummaries.content: The release of the Half-Year Economic and Fiscal Update (HYEFU) sparked a major confrontation during Question Time. The update showed economic growth forecasts have been lowered and the Government's return to surplus is now projected for 2029-30, a year later than previously forecast. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon defended his government's record, pointing to falling inflation, rising business confidence, and projected wage growth as signs of a coming recovery. The Opposition, led by Chris Hipkins, accused the Prime Minister of breaking promises of careful economic management, highlighting the delayed surplus, rising unemployment forecasts, and continued borrowing. The debate also touched on cost-of-living pressures, with a pointed exchange over the price of basic groceries.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins (Leader of the Opposition)
keyExchanges.quote: So what year will the New Zealand Government books, according to the operating balance before gains and losses (OBEGAL) measure, return to surplus?

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (Prime Minister)
keyExchanges.quote: According to the operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses measure (OBEGALx), it's 2028-29. That's our Government's determination.

topicSummaries.topic: Controversial Electoral Bill Restricting Voter Enrolment Passes Final Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law now closes voter enrolment 13 days before election day, a change opponents argue will disenfranchise tens of thousands of voters, particularly the young and transient.
topicSummaries.content: The Electoral Amendment Bill passed its third and final reading, enacting significant changes to New Zealand's voting laws. The Government argued the changes, which include closing enrolment 13 days before an election and banning all sentenced prisoners from voting, are necessary to ensure a timely and efficient vote count and uphold the integrity of the system. The move was fiercely opposed by Labour, the Green Party, and Te Pāti Māori, who condemned it as a form of voter suppression that will make it harder for people to vote and disproportionately affect Māori, Pasifika, and young people. Opposition speakers argued the Government's justification of timeliness was not supported by evidence from the Electoral Commission and that the changes undermine a fundamental democratic right.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government should be ashamed of this bill, because what it does is it makes it harder for New Zealanders to vote, pure and simple. That's the truth.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Paul Goldsmith (Minister of Justice)
keyExchanges.quote: New Zealanders need to get an outcome, so what we're doing is we're fixing the basics and we're giving people a year to get themselves enrolled.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Introduces Two Bills to Replace Resource Management Act
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: This major overhaul of planning laws aims to make it faster and cheaper to build houses and infrastructure by separating environmental protection from land use rules.
topicSummaries.content: The Government introduced two landmark bills, the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill, to replace the 30-year-old Resource Management Act (RMA). Minister Chris Bishop stated the reform will unshackle the country from a failed system by restoring property rights and cutting red tape, estimating it could reduce the number of consents needed by up to 46%. The new system separates land use planning from environmental protection. While the coalition government hailed it as a move to enable growth, housing, and infrastructure, opposition parties raised significant concerns. Labour noted the irony of the government introducing similar legislation to what it had repealed two years prior, while also expressing alarm over the emphasis on property rights and a diminished role for mana whenua. The Green Party and Te Pāti Māori also criticised the weakening of environmental protections and Treaty principles.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Chris Bishop (Minister responsible for RMA Reform)
keyExchanges.quote: The RMA is the root cause of our housing crisis. It's made it difficult and expensive to build infrastructure and energy project that we need, it's tied farmers and growers up in red tape, and it has not protected the environment.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Rachel Brooking (Labour—Dunedin)
keyExchanges.quote: I will not undertake a treatise of where property rights have or have not worked with market economies but will note that property rights do not deal with the issue of common resources such as air, water, and biodiversity.

topicSummaries.topic: Parliament Unites to Condemn Bondi Beach Terror Attack
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: In a rare moment of unity, all party leaders expressed solidarity with Australia and New Zealand's Jewish community, condemning antisemitism and extremism.
topicSummaries.content: Parliamentary business began with a unified motion of condolence for the victims of the antisemitic terrorist attack at Bondi Beach. Leaders from all parties delivered speeches expressing shock and grief, standing in solidarity with Australia and New Zealand's Jewish community. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon condemned the attack as an act of extremism and called for a renewed commitment to tolerance, stating that antisemitism has no place in New Zealand. Other leaders echoed these sentiments, denouncing hatred in all its forms and acknowledging the bravery of first responders and civilians. The House then observed a minute's silence as a mark of respect for the victims.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (Prime Minister)
keyExchanges.quote: Let me be absolutely clear: antisemitism has no place in New Zealand—not now and not ever. Confronting antisemitism is not just about favouring one community over another; in fact, it's actually about upholding the values that protect every minority and enhance all of us.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins (Leader of the Opposition)
keyExchanges.quote: Terrorism is designed to divide us. It is designed to turn us against each other. It is designed to create more polarisation... Terrorism is designed to divide us, and we should never ever buy into that.

conclusion: The day was defined by a stark economic debate and the final passage of a divisive electoral law, setting the stage for major political battles over the economy and democratic rights.
